Maybe — and the bar is higher than most people expect. Charities decline a large share of offered furniture, not out of pickiness but economics: a couch they can't sell in their store costs them disposal fees instead of raising money. So before you book a donation pickup and risk a refused-at-the-door situation, run your couch through the same checklist they will.

## The Checklist Charities Actually Apply

Walk around your couch and answer honestly:

- **No stains, or nothing beyond faint wear.** Visible staining is the most common rejection reason. If you'd hesitate to buy it, so will their customers.
- **No odors.** Smoke, pets, and mildew all disqualify — smell doesn't clean out of foam, and inspectors check.
- **No rips, exposed foam, or broken frame parts.** Small snags on a seam may pass; torn cushions and sagging frames won't.
- **All cushions present, mechanisms working.** Recliners must recline; [sleepers must fold out smoothly](/blog/junk-removal/how-to-dispose-of-a-sleeper-sofa/) with a clean mattress.
- **Completely dry, never water-damaged.** Any history of soaking is disqualifying — moisture means mold risk, and no charity will gamble on it.
- **No pest history.** Bed bugs or evidence of infestation ends the conversation immediately, and honestly disclosing it protects the charity's other inventory.

If you cleared all six: your couch is likely donatable. One or two soft failures (light wear, minor snag) — worth offering with photos and letting the charity decide. Any hard failure (odor, moisture, pests, broken structure) — skip to disposal and don't burn a pickup slot.

## Where to Donate

National organizations with furniture programs — Goodwill, The Salvation Army, Habitat for Humanity ReStore — accept couches at many locations, and some offer scheduled pickup. Availability, standards, and pickup wait times vary by branch, so call your local one rather than relying on national policy pages. Local options are often faster: furniture banks, shelters, and refugee resettlement programs frequently need sofas urgently and inspect pragmatically. Photos-first messaging saves everyone a wasted trip.

Expect pickup scheduling to take anywhere from a few days to a few weeks depending on your area's volunteer and truck capacity — worth building into a move-out timeline.

## If It Doesn't Qualify — or the Timing Doesn't Work

A couch that fails the checklist isn't a donation problem, it's a [removal job](/couch-removal/) — and that's fine. Booked removal takes it from inside your home on your schedule, and through our platform, anything that turns out to be donatable gets offered to charity partners first anyway; you don't have to make the call perfectly. What matters is not letting the couch sit outside "for whoever wants it" — [rain converts a donatable couch into landfill freight](/blog/junk-removal/can-i-leave-a-couch-on-the-curb/) in one wet night.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Will Goodwill or Salvation Army pick up my couch for free?

Many branches offer free scheduled pickup for furniture that meets their condition standards, but programs vary by location. Call your local branch with photos ready — they'll tell you quickly whether it qualifies and how long the pickup wait is.

### Why do charities reject so many couches?

Economics. A couch that won't sell costs the charity disposal fees. Inspectors apply a simple test: would a customer buy this today? Stains, odors, and damage all fail that test.

### Can I donate a couch with pet hair or light pet use?

Hair alone, freshly cleaned, often passes. Pet odor or scratching damage usually doesn't. Deep-vacuum and deodorize first, then be honest in your photos — refused-at-the-door helps no one.

### Is donating a couch really better than disposal?

When it qualifies, clearly yes: it funds charity programs, houses someone's living room, and skips the landfill. Our guide on [what happens to furniture after pickup](/blog/junk-removal/what-happens-to-old-furniture-after-you-get-rid-of-it/) covers the full picture.
